title: Foreign Investors Have Fled 43 of India's 50 Biggest Stocks. Domestic Money Is Filling the Void.
excerpt: FII ownership in Indian equities has plunged to a 14-year low of 14.7 per cent, while domestic institutional holdings have surged to a record 18.9 per cent — a structural shift that reshapes risk and opportunity for NRI investors.
body:
The most significant structural shift in Indian equity ownership in a generation is happening in plain sight, and most NRI investors are only seeing the damage, not the opportunity forming beneath it.

Foreign institutional investors have sold stakes in 43 of India's 50 biggest Nifty stocks this year, pushing aggregate foreign ownership in Indian equities to a 14-year low of 14.7 per cent. At the same time, domestic institutional holdings have climbed to a record 18.9 per cent, according to data from Equirus Securities. The cumulative FII outflows in the first five months of 2026 have already surpassed the total outflows of the entire previous year, reaching nearly ₹2.3 lakh crore — roughly $30 billion.

The Nifty 50 and Sensex have dropped 11 and 13 per cent respectively in 2026, and the Indian rupee has fallen 6 per cent to record lows near ₹97 per dollar. For NRI investors measuring returns in dollars, the combined hit to equity and currency has been punishing.

## What Is Driving the Exodus

Three forces have converged to make India deeply unfashionable with foreign capital.

The first is oil. The Iran-US war that erupted in February has sent Brent crude above $90 per barrel, with periodic spikes to nearly $100. India, the world's third-largest oil importer, is acutely vulnerable. Higher energy costs widen the current account deficit, stoke inflation and compress corporate margins — a triple blow that hits the Indian growth story at its foundation.

The second is AI. South Korea and Taiwan, home to the semiconductor and memory giants riding the artificial intelligence investment boom, have overtaken India in market capitalisation. Foreign investors have rotated aggressively toward chip fabricators, leaving India's market — which lacks a direct AI hardware play — looking like a relic from the pre-AI era.

The third is valuation. India trades at a nearly 40 per cent premium to the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, roughly 3 per cent above its long-term average. Its trailing price-to-earnings ratio has rarely dipped below 21 times since 2022, while Brazil trades at 11 times and South Korea at 17 times. In a risk-off environment, the premium makes India the most obvious source of funds.



> **"BlackRock, which manages more than $14 trillion globally, said this week that India's equity market has been "over-punished" for lacking a direct AI play and for higher oil risks."**


## The Domestic Counterweight

What makes this cycle different from past foreign-selling episodes is the domestic response.

Domestic institutional investors — primarily mutual funds fed by the now-enormous systematic investment plan (SIP) pipeline — have absorbed much of the foreign exit. DII inflows crossed ₹4 lakh crore in 2026, providing a cushion that simply did not exist during the 2008 or 2013 sell-offs.

SIP flows remained remarkably resilient at $3.25 billion in May, barely budging from April despite a month of extreme volatility, falling currency and Iran war headlines. The Indian retail investor, often dismissed as fickle and sentiment-driven, has become the most disciplined participant in the market.

But the cushion has a limit. CLSA analysts warned in a recent note that they are "now seeing the first signs of depletion in the resources of DIIs after 18 months of fighting this battle of equity flows." Cash held by equity mutual funds fell to ₹1.78 trillion at the end of February, down 24 per cent from April 2025.

Equity mutual fund inflows themselves moderated 40 per cent month-on-month in May to ₹229 billion, the lowest in a year. Small-cap, mid-cap and large-cap fund inflows each fell by roughly a third.

## The Contrarian Case

Against this bleak backdrop, some of the world's largest asset managers are quietly turning constructive.

BlackRock, which manages more than $14 trillion globally, said this week that India's equity market has been "over-punished" for lacking a direct AI play and for higher oil risks. Natasha Sarkaria, the firm's EMEA wealth investment strategy lead, called India one of BlackRock's "highest-conviction, medium- to long-term emerging-market trades," supported by demographics, infrastructure spending and indirect AI-linked opportunities.

Lighthouse Canton echoed the view. Chief Investment Officer Abhay Laijawala argued that India's absence from the AI hardware trade could prove an "advantage of absence." While South Korea and Taiwan face concentration risk from their semiconductor-heavy indices, India offers a deep, diversified listed universe tied to the next phase of AI spending: power generation, data centres, cooling systems, engineering and capital goods.

"We have plenty of picks and shovels," Laijawala said.

## What NRI Investors Should Watch

For diaspora investors, the ownership shift carries several practical implications.

First, the FII-to-DII handoff means Indian markets are becoming less vulnerable to the kind of sharp, sentiment-driven foreign outflows that triggered past crashes. A market increasingly owned by domestic capital is a market that reacts more to local earnings and less to global risk-on/risk-off cycles.

Second, the sectors FIIs have abandoned most aggressively — IT, financials and pharmaceuticals — are precisely the sectors that many NRIs hold in their Indian portfolios. Thirteen Nifty stocks have seen FII ownership fall by more than 20 per cent. Whether this represents forced selling or a structural re-rating is the core investment question.

Third, the RBI's recent measures to attract NRI capital — including fully subsidised hedging costs on three-to-five-year foreign currency deposits and higher FCNR rates of up to 7 per cent — are designed to draw dollar inflows precisely when they are most needed. Banks could raise $35 to $40 billion through these deposits by September.

The $30 billion foreign exit from Indian equities in 2026 is the headline. The structural rise of domestic ownership to record levels is the story. For NRI investors watching from abroad, the question is no longer whether to worry about the outflows but whether the foundation being laid by domestic capital is strong enough to invest into.
